Repeated charges expose violence across borders

Each message begins with the same formula of three wrongs and four. None of these nations is charged with breaking Israel’s law. They are charged with cruelty any people would know as wrong. Verse 9 says Tyre handed over a whole community to slavery. It also forgot a treaty of brotherhood. Every charge in the chapter names harm done to human beings. God holds nations to account for such acts.
The accusation turns toward Israel's own worship

Amos’s hearers would have approved the judgments on their neighbors. The eighth message turns on them. Israel’s list is the longest, and it concerns everyday dealings. Verse 6 says people are sold into slavery over small debts. Verse 8 says cloaks taken in pledge are used at the shrines. Exodus 22:26–27 required such a cloak back by sunset. The worship is furnished with the goods of the poor.

Verse 2 has a surprising “Therefore.” Israel might expect its special place to bring safety. God says it brings greater responsibility. Being chosen makes the people answerable. Verses 3–8 then defend Amos’s right to say so. Verse 9 calls foreigners to look at Samaria’s violence. Verse 15 names the many fine houses that will fall.
Religious display continues without a changed response

Verses 4–5 describe worship that is busy and generous. The people “love” to do it. Verses 6–11 list five disasters. Each ends with the same line: “yet you haven’t returned to me.” “Cleanness of teeth” in verse 6 means nothing to eat. Much religious activity goes on, and no one turns. Verse 12 says the next meeting will be with God himself.
Justice must replace confidence in protected worship

The “gate” in verses 10, 12, and 15 is the town’s court. Bribes are taken there, and the needy are turned away. Verses 21–23 then reject the people’s feasts and music. The two belong together. Unfair courts make the worship unwelcome. Verse 24 asks for justice like a stream that never dries. Many streams in that land ran only after rain.
Comfort without grief becomes the first captivity

Verses 4–6 list ivory beds, fine meat, music, wine, and oil. The charge comes in the last line of verse 6. These people feel no grief for the breaking of their nation. Their comfort has made them numb. The penalty fits the description. Verse 1 calls them the “first” of the nations. Verse 7 says they will go “first” into exile.
The priest's royal protection conflicts with Amos's calling

Amaziah’s words show how he thinks. Verse 13 calls Bethel “the king’s sanctuary” and a royal house. Verse 12 treats prophecy as a way to earn bread. Amos answers that he never held that post. He kept flocks and tended trees. Verse 15 says the LORD “took” him, as he took David from the sheep. In verses 2 and 5 this same man pleaded for Israel.
Dishonest markets prepare a different kind of famine

The merchants in verse 5 keep the new moon and the Sabbath. They only wish the days would end. The verse names three frauds in one sale. The measure is small, the weight for payment is heavy, and the scale is rigged. Verse 6 adds that they sell the chaff. They observe the holy day and defeat its purpose. Verses 11–12 take away the word they would not hear.
Destroyed false security gives way to inhabited land

Verse 7 removes Israel’s claim to special treatment. God moved other nations as well. After that, the book ends in promise. In 5:11 the people built houses they would not live in. They planted vineyards and would not drink the wine. Verse 14 reverses both lines exactly. Verse 11 calls David’s house a “tent,” a humble thing raised again.
